candidate_relations.label: Alcoholic cerebellar ataxia
candidate_relations.reason: While alcohol history is present, the progressive course after cessation, palatal myoclonus, and overall syndrome fit PAPT rather than alcoholic cerebellar ataxia. Asserts an incompatible etiology and omits the palatal tremor component.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Attributes ataxia to alcohol etiology; record notes ataxia progressed after cessation of alcohol, and the full syndrome includes palatal tremor/myoclonus not explained by alcoholic cerebellar degeneration alone

candidate_relations.label: Superior Cerebellar Artery Infarction
candidate_relations.reason: No imaging or clinical evidence of infarction; the chronic progressive course is incompatible with a discrete vascular event.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Vascular etiology with acute onset; record describes 20-year progressive course with no mention of stroke

candidate_relations.label: Palatal Myoclonus
candidate_relations.reason: Palatal myoclonus is a key feature documented in the record but is only one component of the full PAPT diagnosis; the broader progressive ataxia syndrome is not captured.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Captures only the palatal tremor component of PAPT; omits the progressive ataxia syndrome and sporadic PAPT designation

candidate_relations.label: Spinocerebellar Ataxia
candidate_relations.reason: Genetic testing explicitly excluded the common SCA subtypes, and the diagnosis does not account for the palatal myoclonus. Asserting SCA conflicts with the negative genetic workup and the full PAPT syndrome.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Genetic SCA subtypes tested (1,2,3,6,12) were all negative; does not include palatal tremor component

case_quality_flags: Reference diagnosis is a rare, well-defined syndrome (PAPT sporadic type); none of the candidates capture the complete composite diagnosis
Alcohol history creates a plausible but explicitly refuted alternative etiology (ataxia worsened after cessation)
